en: *The Ten Profundities of the Lotus Sūtra: The Door of Non-Duality*, Illustrated with the Pearl and the Finger, Volume One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Yuánqīng of Dànqiū.

The crest-jewel of the Dharma King was bestowed upon the Wise One (Zhìzhě) during his liberation at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Having received it, he transmitted and revealed it to others; there are those who possess it.
As for those who have seen it, Master Jingxi pointed it out to them so they might see; yet there were still some who, despite his pointing, were unable to observe it accordingly.
Therefore, I now point once more to that very pointing.
First, the explanation of the title.

The Ten Subtleties of the Lotus Sūtra: The Gate of Non-duality (This title was established by Master Geyan in the sixth fascicle of the *Shiqian* [Commentary on the Profound Meaning], who summarized the general purport of the ten subtleties to directly expound the revelation of the single principle and demonstrate the ultimate limit of what is taught;
thus he coined this name himself). The first seven characters constitute the title established by Master Jingxi based on Zhiyi’s exposition;
the subsequent thirty-two characters are a postscript added by a later person to clarify the meaning of the text.

First, a brief explanation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the scripture upon which this work is based. Its full title is *Miaofa* (the Wondrous Dharma; the "Dharma" itself) *Lianhua Jing* (Lotus Sutra; the "Lotus" is a metaphor). It is here abbreviated as such.

As for the ten "wondrous aspects" (*daśamitha*) fully explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), those designated here as the basis of our reliance are specifically the ten wondrous aspects within the "trace" (*jiji*).
Regarding the "Gate of Non-duality," that which is described from this point onward refers to the gate of the perfect and wondrous nature of the Dharma-body. There is an original [text].
The titles *The Ten Profundities of the Original and Traces of the Lotus Sūtra: The Gate of Non-duality*, *The Lotus Sūtra’s Original and Traces:

The Gate of Non-duality*, *The Ten Profundities of the Original and Traces: The Gate of Non-duality*, or simply *Original and Traces* are all later interpolations and are not used here (this will be clarified in the section on "Questions and Answers").

The second part, the Extensive Explanation, consists of three chapters: first, revealing the true mark of non-dual mind-only; second, revealing the dependent origination of the dharma-realm of delusion and awakening;
third, resolving doubts through questions and answers.

Regarding the first, the revelation of the true mark of non-dual mind-only, this is the revelation that in this sutra, the provisional is opened up to reveal the real, such that all sentient beings are one.
One should contemplate with a mind of submission to the true Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is solely for this purpose:
to cause sentient beings to realize that the ten dharma-realms are entirely one's own mind—the pure essence, the wondrously perfect enlightened nature.

Indeed, these ten dharma-realms are identical to a single thought-moment; they do not arise through prior and subsequent succession, nor do they consist of form containing the internal and external as one.

First, all phenomena are in their very essence True Suchness; how could there be a knower and that which is known? The nature of knowing is itself the substance. All phenomena converge in form (*rūpa*);
this convergence does not transcend form, for form is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The Dharma-realm is mind-only.

All phenomena converge in fragrance, and so on, up to characteristics, nature, substance, function, power, causes, conditions, fruits, and retributions—from the beginning to the end—all are ultimately equal, being none other than the Dharma-realm. One.
The dharma of the single dharma-realm is the wondrous essence of true suchness within a single thought-moment. Furthermore, the essence of this single thought is eternally empty and quiescent;
it is not a state of mental activity for the sake of clarity, nor is it a state of non-activity for the sake of stillness. Thought is itself non-thought, and its very substance cannot be grasped.

All dharmas are from the beginning characterized by eternal quiescence and extinction. There is nothing that can know them as something other than these dharmas; rather, the entirety of all dharmas is, in its totality, a single thought-moment.

The characteristic of the signless within the signless is the true reality. It is like a *maṇi* jewel whose substance is perfectly pure; the entire jewel is not color, yet it is translucent emptiness.
This entire translucent emptiness is the color of the *maṇi*. According to one's wishes, it can rain down all kinds of various jewels.
These jewels do not exist within the jewel, nor do they come from without; for the wondrous substance of the jewel inherently possesses all jewels. Thus it is profound.
The meaning is as follows: When expanded, it fills the Dharma-realm; one does not know from where it comes. When contracted, nothing is known to exist; one does not know where it goes.
One should know that all phenomena are non-dual, being mind-only. Mind-only is without marks, yet it possesses all marks.
Therefore, these ten gates—the phenomena of the ten gates—are all called "non-dual," for each and every phenomenon is, in its very essence, such.
That which penetrates through is called a "gate" (*mukha*). If one dharma enters this [gate], outside of this single dharma there are no further nine gates as distinct entities;
they are all identical to my own single thought of pure, numinous awareness. This is like a single perfect sphere possessing ten apertures, none of which are not that same sphere.
If one aperture is entered, the entire perfect sphere is entered; there is nothing that is not the sphere itself, even regarding the other apertures through which it is entered.

Although each pearl is identical in its essential substance, these ten gates thus allow for mutual penetration; from form and mind down to the moisture they receive, all are made such that the principle of the ten mysteries is one from beginning to end.

(The following demonstrates the non-duality of the six stages of realization; as the text on the pearls states, "under each gate, examine them by means of the six stages," this general summary is provided here.
Throughout various Mahāyāna sūtras, the Buddha has everywhere proclaimed that the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—are without difference.
Within the nature of distinct afflictions, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is fully present; the Tathāgata’s robes, virtues, and marks are complete and without deficiency.
The Buddha-realm and the realm of sentient beings are a single realm with no separate realms; all sentient beings are suchness (*tathatā*).

All phenomena (*dharma*) converge upon form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, and do not transcend this convergence. Form and the other aggregates are all eternal, blissful, self, and pure. All sentient beings...

All living beings possess Buddha-nature; it is like the jewel on a strongman’s forehead—perfectly bright and present within his body—which is the "Buddha in the state of principle" (*riji-butsu*), the non-dual jewel of the mind.

(This refers to the inherent virtue [shōtoku]; the following five refer to cultivated virtue [shutoku]). Furthermore, regarding all the Buddhas of the past, if there were even one who heard a single phrase [of this teaching], there was not one who did not become a Buddha.
If one hears even a single phrase of this sutra, whether during the lifetime of a Buddha or after his parinirvāṇa...
Recalling and rejoicing in all these deeds, one receives the prediction of bodhisattva-hood from the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who preaches this sūtra.
It is like tying a priceless jewel within one’s inner garment;

this is the "jewel of the non-dual mind" that is the Buddha by name (it is called "Buddha by name" because one has previously heard the Buddha's name from within the sūtras and from spiritual friends). Furthermore, one cultivates the gathering of the mind and contemplates the emptiness of all phenomena.
One who studies the Mahāyāna according to the true nature of reality, though possessing only the physical eye, is said to possess the Buddha-eye.

If one wishes to attain all dharmas, one should study Prajñā; it is like obtaining a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). This is the practice of contemplation, the very jewel of the non-dual mind of the Buddha. (Regarding this, there are five grades of practitioners:

first, those who at every thought-moment have faith and understanding—this is the perfect single mind of the three truths; second, those who additionally are able to receive, uphold, and understand Mahāyāna sūtras and commentaries; third, those who further extensively preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings; fourth, those who are able to preach the Dharma.)

Furthermore, those who practice both the six perfections and the five matters, whose principle and mind are harmonized and integrated, and who cultivate the six perfections through all five stages—this is called "Perfect Practice," which is identical to the stage of "Contemplative Practice as the Buddha.

Moreover, those who uphold this sutra attain the purity of the six sense faculties; from the Avīci Hell below to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) above, as well as the physical forms of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas, all appear within their own bodies.
They alone perceive these clearly, while others do not see them. It is, for example, like showing [them]...
The pearl bound to his heart filled him with great joy; this is precisely the "similarity" (xiāngsì) pearl, the non-dual pearl of the Buddha’s mind.

(Regarding the "revealing and clarifying" [kāixiǎn] stage for śrāvakas: because their level is identical to the stage of the six sense organs being pure, they employ the pearl of realization. If they were to advance further, it would be identical to the "partially true" (fēnzhēn) stage, not this present stage. Here, there are ten levels of the mental state; reaching the seventh mental state is the actual stage of the six sense organs being pure.

These ten levels are all "similar" to the partially true, thus sharing the name "similarity-to-Buddhahood" [xiāngsì-jí-fó]). Furthermore, at the time of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one again achieves perfect awakening from the Buddha’s own mouth.

Born from the transformation of the Dharma, one attains a portion of the Buddha-dharma; the Dragon Girl offers her pearl and becomes a Buddha in the South. This is the "True-portion-as-Buddha" (fen-zhen ji-fo), the non-dual mind-pearl.

(The offering of the pearl symbolizes the attainment of perfect understanding (*yuan-jie*) and the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it is not merely a metaphorical illustration. These consist of forty-one stages, all of which involve shattering ignorance and realizing the true mark (*shi-xiang*), yet their wisdom and function are not without degrees of excellence.

The ten abodes (*shizhu*) are called "opening," the ten practices (*shixing*) are called "indicating," the ten transferences (*shihuixiang*) are called "awakening," and the ten grounds (*shidi*) plus Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue*) are called "entering. Although these forty-one stages differ in their beginning and end, they are collectively termed "True-portion-as-Buddha."

Furthermore, beyond the stage of *tathatā* (the wordless), there is that which is named the "Supreme Being" (*uttama-puruṣa*). Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena;
this alone is the single jewel atop the crown of the King. This ultimate state is the "Non-dual Mind-Jewel" of the Buddha. (This refers exclusively to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment.

As for the passages from various sutras clarifying the six levels of "identity," they have not been cited here as the author feared the text would become overly prolix. Regarding the positions of the six levels of identity clarified in the various sutras: [The text continues with the six identities: 1. Identity in principle (*li-jizhi*); 2. Identity in name (*ming-jizhi*); 3. Identity in semblance (*xiang-jizhi*); 4. Identity in practice (*xing-jizhi*); 5. Identity in partial realization (*bu-jizhi*); 6. Ultimate identity (*jijizhi*). (Note: The original text appears to be a commentary on the Tiantai doctrine of the "six identities" (*liu-ji*), explaining the progression from the initial potentiality of Buddhahood to its final, perfect realization.)
In every instance, the ultimate sage is identical from beginning to end, non-dual, and nothing other than a single thought-moment of the pure *maṇi* jewel.
Outside this single thought-moment there is no Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no self-mind. Therefore, the *Vajrasūcī* states:

"The environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely within the self-mind of the ultimate sage; the body and land of Vairocana do not exceed a single thought-moment of the ordinary person. This is shown to be so...

Second, having established that the true reality is solely mind, [the text] secondly demonstrates the dependent origination of the dharma-realm regarding delusion and awakening: all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have inherently possessed the ten realms of phenomena within a single thought-moment;
they are pure, perfect, and profound, yet because their delusion has been without beginning, it is called "original delusion. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"All dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding" (this refers to sentient beings' beginningless and constant creation [of karma], not that they are suddenly created midway;

these two phrases are cited here to provide the foundation for the "pure dependent origination" discussed below). The "root of non-abiding" is the essence of a single thought-moment which is eternally empty and quiescent;

because its original nature cannot be grasped and it has no point of reliance, it is called the "root of non-abiding. Non-abiding is itself the root. (The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Because the dharma-nature is precisely ignorance, the dharma-nature is non-abiding; ignorance... )

Because it is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), ignorance is non-existent; here, we simply point directly to its essence. This is the root of non-abiding that contains all phenomena, and is therefore called *dharmatā*.

Because this nature is inherently complete, through conditions it can give rise to the defiled—defiled conditions giving rise to defiled phenomena—and through conditions it can give rise to the pure—pure conditions giving rise to pure phenomena.

It is like a fire-gem or a water-gem: when turned toward the sun, it produces fire; when turned toward the moon, it produces water. Yet a single round gem possesses the natures of both fire and water. The sun... [is merely the condition].

The single thought-mind that is able to arise by virtue of the moon is also like this. (The above section clarifies both defilement and purity through analogy and principle; below, first purity is clarified, followed by defilement.

Just as all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been consistently unaware and are constantly subject to defiled conditions—namely, the conditions of ignorance and karma—they may create various karmas and fully experience the retribution of suffering;
therefore, there exist earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch.
The *Great Treatise on the Dharmas of the Three Realms, the Supported and the Supporting* states: "There are no separate dharmas in the three realms; they are created solely by the one mind.

Because of inversion, one does not know that it is only the mind; instead, following conditions, one contrarily creates [phenomena], claiming them to be external objects, thereby giving rise to attachment and aversion, grasping at objects, and wandering through longing and detachment.
Thus one flows and turns through the six destinies, the four modes of birth, the ten modes of birth, and the twelve links of dependent origination, circling without end."
In the state of nirvāṇa, it is like a king who, while enjoying himself at a springtime pond, suddenly drops a bright pearl into its depths.

When the people hear of this, they all enter the pond; each grasps a piece of tile or rubble, believing they have found the precious pearl. (This refers to the three types of cultivation in the preliminary expedients.

This parable illustrates how beings forget the cause and effect [of their own minds]. Vimalakīrti wishes to lead sentient beings to realize that the fundamental nature is "mind-only," the true essence of non-abiding.

One immediately realizes that all phenomena produced by inversion are nothing other than mind-only; thus it is said, "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established" (this refers to the defiled conditions).
If sentient beings, from time immemorial, encounter pure conditions (the conditions of teaching and practice), they immediately attain Buddhahood.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddhas, the Honored Ones with Two Feet, know that dharmas are eternally without self-nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. This is so.
Therefore, it is said that the One Vehicle is eternally without self-nature; this refers to the true Buddha-nature seed which is the foundation of non-abiding.
There are three causes for this: Buddha-nature is itself the seed. First, the direct cause (dharmatā-hetu): the suchness (*tathatā*) of sentient beings is inherently pure in its essential substance;

this is the nature of Vairocana, termed the "seed of the Dharma-body" (which corresponds to the aforementioned retribution of suffering). Second, the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*): the natures of greed, anger, and ignorance are fundamentally luminous and clear.

The nature of *prajñā* is called the seed of the *saṃbhogakāya* (which is the aforementioned delusion); the nature of the three conditions is the nature of karma in the six destinies, which is unattainable;
this is the nature of liberation, called the seed of the *nirmāṇakāya* (which is the aforementioned aspect of karma).

For example, a *maṇi* jewel has but a single perfect form (metaphor for the *dharmakāya*), gold beads are translucent (metaphor for *prajñā*), and all its various treasures (metaphor for liberation)—these three are one in character, neither identical nor different.
"Differentiation arising from conditions" refers to these three causes, whose nature and seeds both arise from the conditions of teaching and practice. As the *Sūtra on Dependent Origination* states:
"If there is one who hears even a single phrase, there is not one who will not become a Buddha"—this is dependent origination through the teaching.

If a son of good family can, regarding this sūtra, for even a single moment rejoice in it, or even with a profound mind believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe it...

To cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, culminating in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*), is called the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā-vyūha*).

This is the seed of *prajñā* (which reverses the previous state of delusion). As the Sūtra says: "Bowing the head, raising the hand, drawing on the ground, or gathering sand—all these lead to the path of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, the *Caryā-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra* states: "If a son of good family abides in patience, giving rise to gentleness, kindness, and compliance..."
Yet there is no sudden violence, nor is the mind alarmed. Sons of the Buddha who dwell in this stage are those whom the Buddha accepts as his own;
having practiced these various paths, they shall become Buddhas in future ages. This is called the Adornment of Merit, which manifests liberation (reversing the characteristics of prior karma).
As the Sūtra says: "All sentient beings are my children; all who possess a mind shall attain Buddhahood. My own mind..."

Emptiness means that sin and merit have no master; one should contemplate that the entire dharma-realm is solely mind. By pulverizing the mind into atoms, one reveals the great thousand-fold sutra-scrolls.

The power of samādhi and wisdom, adorned according to what is attained, constitutes the true causal nature—the True Dharmakāya which is the object of adornment (reversing the aforementioned retribution of suffering).
This is the arising of the three causal natures of the Buddha-seed through the teaching and practice of the One Vehicle.

Therefore it is said: "The seed of the Buddha arises from conditions; for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. Thus, the wisdom capable of awakening possesses its own degrees of depth and shallowness.
For example, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, when contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination according to the fourfold teaching, there are four types of wisdom:

with inferior wisdom, one contemplates but does not see the Buddha-nature and attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; with middling wisdom, one contemplates but does not see the Buddha-nature and attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
When one observes with superior wisdom but does not see clearly, one attains the bodhi of a bodhisattva;

when one observes with the most superior wisdom, one immediately sees the Buddha-nature and attains the bodhi of a Buddha (the four wisdoms correspond to the four teachings as explained in the *Xuanyi*). It is like a multicolored cloth wrapping a maṇi jewel:

its light changes according to the colors, appearing as dark blue, yellow, or other hues. Thus, the light perceived by those of the two vehicles follows their conditions; [the Buddha] takes pity on them for their failure to perceive its original substance.
At the assembly of Nirvana, [the Buddha] earnestly directed his gaze toward them, commanding them to contemplate deeply the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

All saw the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). Buddha-nature is called the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*); emptiness is called the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*); the Middle Way is called the Buddha; and the Buddha is called Nirvana.

(The following section translates the preceding earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and the triple world of the environment and its inhabitants. Nirvana is permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), and the true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the ground of nature, the original self-nature of true emptiness, and the aspect of form.

(The true Dharma-realm-nature fire is true emptiness, without marks or touch); I (the true Dharma-realm-nature wind is true emptiness, without marks or taste); Pure (the true Dharma-realm-nature water is true emptiness, without marks or fragrance).

Because the body and land of Vairocana are of one essence—the dependent and the supported—within the secret treasury of the three virtues, it is said that "I place all children within the secret treasury.

I, too, shall not long remain apart, but will dwell therein myself. This is precisely the meaning of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* which states: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. This is the reality of this intent.

If one can thus deeply contemplate and perceive the secret treasury of the true Buddha-nature, one should know that the characteristics and substance of the ten dharma realms are equal, fundamentally without decrease or increase, and that the three periods of time are boundless and not separate from the mind of a single thought.
Because the nature of the ten realms is the eternally tranquil, true *tathatā*, the Sūtra says: "This Dharma abides in its own place; the characteristics of the world are eternal."

Having completed the section on abiding in the demonstration of the dharma-realm of dependent origination regarding delusion and enlightenment, the third section concerns resolving doubts through questions and answers. Question:

Regarding the statement that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated, does one say "three" because the mind differs from sentient beings and Buddhas, or does one say "three" because cause and effect differ? Answer: Now, "Buddha" is named for true contemplation (*bhūta-darśana*), while "sentient beings" is named for...
The unawakened mind is itself the mind that gives rise to Buddhas; there is no mind apart from that which gives rise to Buddhas.

Since the mind is the very foundation of both birth-and-death and Buddhahood, the sutras demonstrate that the fundamental and the derivative, cause and effect, are non-dual. Thus it is said that "the three are without distinction," as explained extensively in the *Sūtra on the Parable of the Sons* and its commentaries.

Now, relying on our own school, we shall briefly indicate the profound meaning of cause and effect. In the *Commentary*, it is explained that there are three aspects of phenomena: 1. The Phenomenal Aspect (*sāṃvṛtika-dharma*). 2. The Ultimate Aspect (*paramārtha-dharma*). 3. The Aspect of the True Nature (*dharmatā-dharma*). [End of excerpt]

This means that regarding the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings, if one determines their causal relationship: the nature of the mind is definitively situated in the cause; the nature of the Buddha is definitively situated in the fruit;
and the nature of sentient beings, according to the general sense, applies to both cause and fruit. As for the mind being defined as the cause: the mind itself is neither cause nor fruit;
rather, it is designated as the "cause" based on its capacity to produce all phenomena. Why is this? As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All..."
"Mind-only creates; the mind creates all Tathāgatas and so forth. Is it not the case that the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms are all created by the mind?

Because the cause can bring about the fruit, it is called the "definite cause. As for the Buddha as the "definite fruit," because one awakens to one's own mind through cultivation and study to the ultimate degree, one is named "Buddha";
therefore, it is called the "definite fruit. That sentient beings, in a general sense, encompass both cause and fruit is due to the beginningless origin.

Deluded beings do not realize that their own minds are pure; they perceive the essence [of the mind] as constantly pursuing delusive conditions to create various delusive karmas—this is called the "delusive cause"—and they undergo various delusive designations—this is called the "delusive effect.
Therefore, it is said that, taken in one sense, this principle pervades both cause and effect.

However, when viewed from the perspective of the Buddha’s true fruition (the second sense), it pertains only to the cause; for this reason, even the Buddha is "mind-only," and cause and effect are non-dual.
Therefore, it is said that there is no difference.
Question: If sentient beings have been fundamentally deluded since beginningless time and are necessarily distinct from the Buddha, does the Buddha awaken from this very delusion?

If he does not awaken from delusion, then there would be a "spontaneous" Buddha who is different from sentient beings. If he must indeed awaken from delusion, then [the analogy of] "supposing there were none... [applies].
Originally, before the Buddhas had attained awakening, who established these teachings and provided the conditions for the vehicles?

If it is said that sentient beings can awaken by themselves because the Buddha’s eye of wisdom is inherently possessed within the mind, then why do all sentient beings not possess this awakened nature and yet fail to awaken on their own?
Why must they rely on the conditions of the vehicles? Furthermore, since the beginningless past has no limit, who could [have established them]?
To resolve these various doubts in their entirety, I shall provide an explanation. Answer: This arises because the realm of the Buddhas is not something that can be fathomed by ordinary beings.

Nevertheless, the Sūtra states that those who study the Mahāyāna, though possessing only the fleshly eye, are said to possess the Buddha-eye and are thus able to know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, based on the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), one may infer this; if one wishes to reach the primordial limit of beginninglessness, [one must rely upon such teachings].
This is precisely what is meant by "a single thought-moment. Why? The *Shorter Prajñāpāramitā* states: "The past mind cannot be apprehended; the present mind cannot be apprehended;
the future mind cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they are the basis of non-abiding;
non-abiding is itself beginninglessness. Although they cannot be apprehended, the nature of a single thought-moment is eternally numinous and eternally quiescent. Thus says Master Li.
People say that the ten thousand ages of past and present do not shift from the single moment of the present thought; the Great Master said that thirty kalpas are but a single thought.
If one understands this single thought as being without beginning, what doubt can there be?

Since it is granted that sentient beings are fundamentally the Buddha’s eye of wisdom, even if this has been so since the beginningless past, how could a single Buddha’s self-awakening contradict this? It is like a Pratyekabuddha remaining among ordinary people.
If one can yet personally realize that causes and conditions are subject to change and transition in order to realize the Holy Path, how much more so for the Buddhas?

Furthermore, since the capacities and natures of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions are unequal—some being sharp and others dull—even if there were someone of sharp wisdom from time immemorial who could spontaneously awaken to the fact that all dharmas are merely this, and thus achieve Buddhahood through sudden cultivation, would this not mean that all dharmas are themselves the True Teaching? As it is said: [The text continues with a citation].
The Sūtra states that all dharmas are the Mahāyāna; cultivating one's livelihood and engaging in productive industry is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

A single form and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way. Furthermore, as in the Buddha-lands where the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are fully utilized, upon seeing forms, hearing sounds, or experiencing touch, one attains awakening to the Way.
Therefore, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) explains that a single character of the Sūtra pervades all six sense objects.
Since every single phenomenon, in every atom, is the wondrous *Sūtra of the True Dharma Realm*, the text concludes with this praise:
"One who understands the characters in this way does not hold a scroll in hand yet is always reading the sūtras; though no sound issues from the mouth, one recites all the scriptures universally;

though the Buddha does not preach the Dharma, one constantly hears the Brahma-voice; though the mind does not engage in discursive thought, it universally illumines the Dharma-realm—is this not the thorough comprehension of all phenomena?"

Mind-only arises from the mind’s inherent nature; by shattering the subtle dust of the mind, the Great Thousand-fold Sūtra emerges. The *Garbha-sūtra* states: "The Dharma-nature is like a great ocean;
it does not say that there are such things as ordinary beings or sages. It is equal and without high or low; it depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements.

To attain realization is as easy as turning over one's hand. If this is so, what prevents the single Buddha of beginningless time from attaining self-awakening and transmitting it through successive generations?

As for transforming others, those whose faculties are dull are unable to awaken on their own; this is truly because, from time immemorial, they have been steeped in attachment to all phenomena, constantly dwelling in birth and death, accumulating various karmas, and being heavily burdened by ignorance and delusion.

Therefore, the Buddhas, out of great compassion, establish various skillful means—such as the wooden ox, the willow leaves, the illusory city, and the precious destination—to serve as the causal conditions for teaching and practice. This is the Lotus Sūtra.
The Record states: "If one traces back to the beginningless past, there must have been a Buddha; yet to fear falling into the error of infinite regress is unwarranted.
Furthermore, one should believe that in the past there was necessarily a Buddha who spontaneously awakened to the Way. It is like a group of blind people wishing to cross a perilous path:

if among them one blind person’s eyes suddenly open and become clear, they can lead the rest across the treacherous terrain. Those who do not follow will fall into the abyss—who would blame the guide?"
This is an error. The Tathāgata established these teachings to instruct those who are like the blind, so that they may understand it.

Question: Since sentient beings have been without beginning, is their single-moment fundamental nature pure? If it is not awakened to, it is called delusion; is it because this single moment is fundamentally illusory that it is called delusion?
Furthermore, many sūtras and śāstras state that sentient beings arise from the True to produce delusion, as in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

It is said that the nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect; this limpid perfection of awakening is fundamentally subtle and wondrous. Fundamental luminosity shines forth, giving rise to the "object," and once the object is established, its own nature perishes.

Through delusive confusion, empty space arises, and based upon space, the world is established. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "All dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding. And as the *Awakening of Faith* says:
"From the gate of True Suchness, through the unchanging yet conforming to conditions, there arise characteristics such as birth and extinction. How could this be...?

Is it not the case that all [phenomena] arise from the True to produce the delusive? If this were so, then the arising of the delusive would have a beginning; how then could one speak of "beginningless fundamental delusion"?
Furthermore, if the fundamental is already the True, why would the True give rise to delusion? Would there still be a need to cease delusion and return to the True? Answer:
This is precisely the Buddha’s teaching on the arising of conditions (*pratyaya*); one must not dogmatically cling to it as being either True or delusive. Why? Because the Buddha, wishing to...
To cause all sentient beings to realize that delusion is itself reality, it is said that "delusion arises from reality.
If the Buddha were to appear in the world and speak directly, saying, "All dharmas have from the beginning been eternally characterized by quiescence;

this is the abiding nature of dharmas, and the characteristics of the world are eternally constant," how could sentient beings be transformed? It would be like saying, "If I were to recite the Buddha-vehicle for the masses..."
Being born and perishing within suffering, is it not true that they are incapable of hearing this Dharma? Nevertheless, by the power of skillful means, he speaks in accordance with sentient beings.

As stated in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), there are three kinds of intentional language (*saṃdhā-bhāṣita*): first, speech according to the Buddha’s own intention, which expounds the Perfect and Sudden Vehicle by directly stating that all phenomena are but the mind, the Dharma-realm, neither real nor false; yet sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been unable to [realize this] themselves.

Jue (Jizang) calls this "delusive flowers," while the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all is created solely by the mind. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says:
"Sentient beings, from time immemorial, have merely attached themselves to various phenomena, thereby wandering in saṃsāra; they do not understand the nature of these phenomena.

Is it not the case that because sentient beings do not understand 'mind-only,' they are turned by those [phenomena]? The Bodhisattva [Zhiyi] composed this treatise to also proclaim this teaching of the Buddha."

The two aspects of the mind—those that accord with one's own intention and those that accord with the intentions of others—and the speech that accords with conditions, as well as their various distinctions, are explained through the eight, nine, and so forth, consciousnesses;
the differentiation between defilement and purity, delusion and awakening, is utterly distinct, and the stages of practice, realization, cause, and fruit are vastly different.

Thus, Bodhisattvas composed various treatises to further elucidate this intent of the Buddha. Yet, there are those who study these sutras and treatises but fail to realize that these are the Buddha’s responses to conditions.

The teaching that emphasizes the partiality of attachment and contention—namely, the view that the faculties, bodies, and the vessel-world of sentient beings must necessarily be produced from the seeds of the eight consciousnesses, such as the seeds of consciousness itself—is judged by the Great Master Zhiyi to belong to the provisional and non-definitive teachings.

He extensively refutes this, showing it shares the same fallacies as the non-Buddhist doctrine of the "Primordial Darkness" (*ādikṛta*) giving rise to "Awakening" (*buddhi*). Third, speech according to the intentions of others refers exclusively to the teaching of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
This refers to the teachings of the Four Āgamas and other such works; likewise, the various sages and saints also composed treatises to expound this intention of the Buddha.

These three types of intentional speech (*saṃdhābhāṣya*) are all teachings given prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to meet the needs of specific conditions. However, once the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* opens up the provisional and reveals the real, all dharmas are seen as the true aspect;
it causes all sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).

Regarding "speech according to one's own intent," there is no inclusion of other categories; rather, it refers to the various dharmas such as "confrontation" and "association," which are fully contained within the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation). Each of these should be examined individually to distinguish the partial from the perfect, so that they may be understood.

Question: The previous exposition of the "Mind-Only True Reality" begins with ordinary beings and culminates in the state of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*). This reduction [of all phenomena] to non-duality—

Question: Does one enter the higher stage simply by contemplating that all is mind-only, or must one further cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom? Answer: Simply contemplating non-duality is itself the cultivation of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration;

to have nothing to transgress is precept; and the wondrous wisdom capable of such contemplation is wisdom. This is called the practice of the Tathāgata, wherein a single practice encompasses them all.
"All practices are carried out" (as explained at length in the "Five Perfect Practices" section of the *Xuanyi*).
Question: When one attains entry into the higher stages through the perfect cultivation of non-duality, is this accomplished in a single lifetime or over many lifetimes?

If it is accomplished over many lifetimes, how does this differ from the gradual approach? If it is accomplished in a single lifetime, who among those present are the ones who have heard of non-duality and achieved this? Answer:
There are three types of persons: First, those whose faculties are extremely sharp, whose afflictive obstructions are somewhat light, whose past cultivation is profound, and whose resolve is firm;

they understand immediately upon hearing [the teaching] and attain sudden realization and entry. This refers to one who realizes the ultimate truth (paramārtha) by means of the conventional world (loka).

Second, those whose faculties are also sharp and whose afflictive obstructions are also light, yet whose past cultivation is not extensive and whose resolve is still weak; they understand immediately upon hearing...

The understanding gained through hearing, reflection, and cultivation should be viewed as realizing that a single thought-moment is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; only then does one attain entry into realization.

This reaches the stage of "teaching for others," wherein one awakens to the primary truth (*paramārtha*). Although their faculties may be sharp, their afflictive obstructions are quite heavy, their past planting of roots of merit is particularly meager, and they lack any aspiration whatsoever.
Because their faculties are sharp, they gain understanding through hearing; yet because their evil is powerful, they follow conditions as they encounter objects.
Only through deep cultivation of both principle and phenomena, and various forms of training and refinement, does one attain entry;

this is the comprehensive application of remedies to awaken to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). (This third person possesses the four *siddhāntas*; however, these four are not necessarily sequential, but are applied according to the capacity of the recipient as they hear them.

Thus, in the parable of the physician’s son and in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, regarding the flowing water that cures illness, there are those who are cured immediately upon merely hearing its description, and there are those to whom it is actually administered.
The phrase "the wondrous medicine successfully eliminates [the illness]" clarifies its underlying meaning.

Although these three types of people differ, they all possess the *yuan-dun* (sudden and perfect) root-nature and have entered stages such as the five ranks (*wupin*) and the ten levels of faith (*shixin*). (Those such as Nanyue and Tiantai were eminent monks of this caliber. As the Sūtra says:

"One who quiets the mind and reaches the source is therefore called a śramaṇa. And as the Treatise says: "Such a noble and wondrous person is one who can see Prajñāpāramitā"—this refers to such individuals.

Furthermore, as for those who are dull-witted and deluded, the poisonous vapor penetrates deeply so that they cannot understand it upon hearing it; even if they do understand, they reject it, thereby creating the cause for the "poisonous drum" and becoming bound by its conditions.

Question: Since you employ skillful means to refine and train [the mind] in various ways, this is already a progression through the stages (*bhūmi*); why then is it called the "Contemplation of Mind-Only Non-duality"?

Answer: It is precisely because all dharmas are fundamentally mind-only that the signs of the world are eternally abiding. From the first step to the seventh step at the site of enlightenment, what is the use of vain deliberation?
Why would one fail to attain awakening through the engagement with phenomena?

Question: If it is as you say—that the distinctions between the ten realms arise from the differences in the perfuming of defiled and pure conditions due to delusion since beginningless time—then these realms are caused by delusion.

How can it be said that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding"? Answer: Even if the ten realms are established based on delusion and awakening, their fundamental source is solely the Mind.
How could this prevent them from being eternally abiding? Is it because the characteristics of form undergo formation and destruction that one would cause [the Mind] to be non-abiding? It is not so.
If even empty space undergoes formation and destruction along with material forms, how much more so for the ten dharma realms? Their nature is fundamentally suchness;
the aspect of total reality that is ultimately ungraspable is itself the true aspect. Since this fundamental aspect is eternally abiding, how could there be any beginning or end?

Question: Since good and evil matters differ and the conditions for delusion and awakening are distinct, is it not the case that defiled conditions have existed from the beginningless past while pure conditions continue to arise?

Answer: Since the two natures are fundamentally eternal, both types of conditions are inherently present; thus, while delusion is fundamentally co-existent with its conditions, the conditions for awakening merely occur sequentially.

Question: Is it the case that delusion necessarily severs wholesome roots while awakening necessarily severs unwholesome ones? Answer: The icchantika does not sever innate wholesome roots (*prakṛti-kuśala-mūla*), but they do sever acquired wholesome roots (*bhāvanā-kuśala-mūla*).
Because they sever acquired wholesome roots, they possess only the adornment of acquired unwholesomeness; thus, they constantly dwell in the evil destinies.

However, because they do not sever innate wholesome roots, should they encounter pure conditions, those innate wholesome roots can be activated, enabling them to reach Bodhi. Furthermore, the Buddha does not sever innate unwholesomeness, yet he does sever [acquired unwholesomeness].
Because one cultivates the severance of evil and is adorned solely by goodness, one abides in the unsurpassed path.
Because one does not sever the nature of evil, one can manifest bodies from the remaining dharma-realm to respond to the various evil destinies;
yet because these are fully understood through awakening, evils do not arise—just as gold extracted from ore cannot become ore again (as detailed in the *Guan-yin xuan-yi*).
Question: If the severing of evil matters is itself the destruction of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), why is it said that ignorance and craving are not extinguished, yet clarity and liberation arise?
Answer: According to the *Yuanzhong lun* (Treatise on the Perfect Center), there is neither severance nor non-severance in severance.

Since one has awakened to the fact that all phenomena are fundamentally only the Self (*ātman*), all manner of evils are themselves gates of samādhi; how could there be any further phenomenon to be called "evil"?
Question: If that is so, there should be only one abandonment; why then are there six distinct types of "subduing-abandonment"? Answer: It is like turbid water whose source is deep and far away;
when driven by a violent wind, fish and dragons emerge and submerge, making it difficult to clear suddenly.

Only after long settling will the myriad forms appear. The abandonment of evil is likewise: although one may suddenly realize that the turbid water of afflictions is, by its very nature, the clarity of *bodhi*.

Water has no beginning, yet its source—the habitual tendencies of past evil—is profound and far-reaching. One must cease the winds of deluded thought and still the fish and dragons of discursive observation;

only then will the true water of *dharmatā* become clear, and the hundreds of thousands of *samādhis* manifest. Therefore, a beginner must understand that deluded thoughts and the true mind are one and the same.

Although the body is pure and its essence is known, because of long-standing habitual tendencies, the mind may still race through a profusion of discursive speech; yet one must always remain aware of this.

When the mind constantly arises and suddenly becomes clear, the "root of name" is purified; further realizing that the nature penetrates to the source and is luminous, this is called "shattering ignorance.

(The speed [of this process] is like the three types of people mentioned previously. One should know that for a person of perfect realization, evil is immediately good; there is truly nothing to be severed, yet one speaks of severance.
This is like Aṅgulimāla, who when encountering adverse conditions, acted wantonly in killing and was thereafter called an "evil man."
When meeting the Buddha, one hears the Dharma of the Reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) and suddenly awakens to the fact that all is but mind, thereby becoming a Great Bodhisattva;

the woman Vāsukī manifested the practice of evil dharmas; and even various spiritual friends manifested as great pits, mountains of knives, and forests of swords—these are all gateways to the wondrous samādhi of the reduction [of phenomena], for they all profoundly penetrate the lack of intrinsic nature in both sin and merit, entering the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of good and evil.
Thus one attains this wondrous function.

Question: Is Vimalakīrti’s teaching that all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding the same as the passage in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* beginning with "The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect" and continuing through "awareness and cognition are identical to those of sentient beings"?
Answer: This merely represents a difference between the perspectives of following and opposing [the flow of phenomena]. Why? Because in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*,...

Because the Buddha had shown Ānanda that all dharmas—the earth, water, and wind—pervade the dharma-realm and are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, which is your own true mind and pure enlightened nature, Pūrṇa then asked the Buddha:

"If the source of all dharmas is fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, how is it that mountains, rivers, the great earth, and so forth suddenly arise? At that time, the Buddha extensively [explained] for him...
Pūrṇa demonstrated that the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous and that fundamental awakening is luminously wondrous;

he explained how, due to the beginningless non-awakening of sentient beings, the false gives rise to objects, resulting in the distinctions between mountains, rivers, the great earth, and sentient beings, as well as providing a detailed analysis of the container-world and the twelve classes of living beings.
He then commanded each of the disciples to speak of their own causes for awakening, presenting their respective original understandings.

The twenty-five methods of perfect penetration were established; subsequently, Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the ten directions mutually emitted light, which descended as an empowerment upon the entire great assembly, causing the ten directions to diminish until they became a single world of the color of the seven treasures.
He then commanded Mañjuśrī to contemplate these twenty-five dharma-gates of perfect penetration. Mañjuśrī immediately spoke verses before the Buddha, as follows:

In what you have shown, it is stated that Pūrṇa’s beginningless delusion regarding the nature of true awakening follows illusory conditions to give rise to the appearances of mountains, rivers, and so forth;
thus it says, "The nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid and perfect," and so on.

Furthermore, among the twenty-five methods of perfect penetration, you specifically selected Avalokiteśvara as the gateway to the non-duality of the true and the simulated, perfect penetration. Is this not also first demonstrating how delusion regarding the truth arises?

When the manifestation of falsely cultivated karma appears, there are false dharmas; only when one settles into each respective teaching of perfect penetration is it that the falsity is realized as the true, which is the meaning of returning to the Tathāgata-garbha.
This is like the case in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, where the Buddha sent Mañjuśrī because Vimalakīrti was manifesting illness.

When asked about the source of his illness, Vimalakīrti replied that its origin arises from delusion (*mṛṣā*). By tracing delusion back to its root, one reaches the foundation of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-mūla*).
Is this not precisely the process of tracing back from delusion to return to the truth? Thus it is clear that non-abiding demonstrates that delusion is itself truth.

One should know that both sutras reveal the fundamental reality of all phenomena as the perfectly eternal *dharmadhātu*; the essence of the scriptures in both cases is identical, and both sutras belong to the Vaipulya class.
The "sections" (or schools) merely contrast the limited with the expansive; they are simplified expositions for the sake of the Three Vehicles and are not the ultimate teaching.
Question: Since all phenomena are fundamentally the treasury of true awakening and are thus non-dual, one should enter this truth through silence, as Vimalakīrti did.
Are these explicit teachings of today not, therefore, also a true entry? Answer: Although the explicit and the silent differ, that which is entered remains no different.

The Great Master Zhi said: "Because the various Bodhisattvas enter through verbal expression for the sake of transforming others, Mañjuśrī—acting as both a model for his own practice and for the transformation of others—demonstrates the entry into the wordless by means of words.

Vimalakīrti, however, because he practices only for himself, neither uses verbal expression nor demonstrates the wordless through words; he enters in silence alone. Therefore, Mañjuśrī praised him as having entered truly."

It is also as in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, where Mahāmati asks the Buddha: "As the World-Honored One has said, from the time of first attaining the Way until reaching Nirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interim.
Based on what secret teaching did the World-Honored One speak these words?

The Buddha replied: "I rely on two secret teachings: first, the Dharma of self-realization; second, the Dharma of abiding in the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Regarding the Dharma of self-realization, it is like being...

"What the Tathāgata has attained, I too have attained. Regarding the "primordially abiding dharma" (*mūlasthita-dharma*), it refers to the primordially existing *dharmadhātu* that is eternally present, just as when one proceeds toward a city by way of a path, the city is reached by means of that path (and so forth). Thus, this eternally abiding *dharmadhātu* is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) and is without fixed abode; this is called "primordial abiding.

To awaken to this mind-only, to accord with the eternal, and to harmonize with the Path is called "self-realization" (*svasaṃvedana*). Therefore, know that self-realization is the cultivation of the primordial.

The dwelling as defined by realization is also consistent with the intent of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. "The luminous subtlety of original enlightenment" (*benjue mingmiao*) refers to self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*).

"The subtle luminosity of intrinsic awareness" (*xingjue miaoming*) refers to the fundamental dwelling. This is also found in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, which clarifies that which the Tathāgata has exhausted:

"nature" (*xing*) is the nature (*prakṛti*), and "Tathāgata" is cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The present sutra states: "The marks of the world are eternally abiding; one knows this at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."
These teachings—such as "this dharma does not function" and "this cannot be shown"—all clarify that cultivation and nature are non-dual;
they are identical in intent to what Vimalakīrti entered. Whether manifest or silent, these are thus demonstrations of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
Question: Is this the same as [the practice of] *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? Answer: The Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā* has three types:

gradual (*anupūrva*), indeterminate (*aniyata*), and sudden-perfect (*yugapat-aikāntika*). As for the gradual: although one understands the perfect principle, the practice is gradual; that is, one cultivates the four dhyānas and eight samādhis in sequence, practicing the refinement through cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, as well as the nine kinds of great dhyānas.

Because these do not arise from the perfect [nature], they are called "gradual. As for the indeterminate: although one practices according to the gradual gate, the arising [of realization] does not proceed solely from the perfect; it may arise suddenly, or gradually, or with the gradual and sudden arising alternately. This is because the seeds of the gradual and sudden have matured due to past habituation. Furthermore, this differs from the perfect [nature].

The arousal of the ten internal objects is merely the mutual manifestation of afflictions and so forth. This "Gate of Non-duality" accords solely with the meaning of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun); thus the text says:

"Therefore, I have extracted the Ten Profound Mysteries (shi-miao) as the general framework for the method of contemplation... when this and that illuminate one another, the practice of the Lotus Sūtra is accomplished;

such a practitioner is one who practices the Lotus Sūtra," which refers precisely to the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (zhiguan). The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Relying upon the sūtras, one opens up the subtle understanding."

To cultivate the three contemplations within a single mind in their perfect unity: those with sharp faculties enter immediately upon hearing the name, like a swift horse that, seeing the shadow of the whip, at once enters the correct path.
Those with heavy obstructions, however, must first contemplate "mind-only" so that their past habitual tendencies may move and various objects manifest;
thus, the Great Master Zhiyi causes them to realize, one by one, that nothing is not mind-only, thereby settling the mind in the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) of samādhi and prajñā.
Therefore, the treatise extensively explains the four samādhis as the gate of practice (*xingmen*), while the ten objects and ten vehicles constitute the method of contemplation (*guānfǎ*).

Regarding the four samādhis: first, constant walking; second, constant sitting; third, half-walking and half-sitting; fourth, neither walking nor sitting (this fourth is also called "following one's own intention" [suízìyì], which encompasses both good and evil movements and is not restricted to a single activity).

These four are all termed *samādhi*—the word *san* means "correct" and *mèi* means "concentration" (*dìng*). Furthermore, the character *san* signifies "clarity" and *mèi* signifies "stillness. Clarity is the essence of contemplation (*guān*), and stillness is the essence of cessation (*zhǐ*); they are thus wondrous concentration and wondrous wisdom. These are the four samādhis.
These four names are obtained according to the functions of those respective objects; they are all merely the One Practice Samādhi.
Because one encounters objects and rides upon them through nothing other than the single mind’s threefold contemplation—the gate of non-duality—it is said that they are identical to this.

Question: If that is so, since the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) is a single treatise solely for the Perfect and Sudden practice, why did Guifeng judge it by saying, "Tiantai’s interpretation is difficult to penetrate;
though the principle is perfect and subtle, the gate of entry is still that of the former methods of entering meditative concentration"? Answer:

What Guifeng said likely refers to his having briefly perused the *Zhenguan zhi guan* (Gradual Cessation and Contemplation); perhaps he had also seen the Perfect and Sudden [version], but [his statement] was based on the former.

The practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* must necessarily involve detailed examination of arising and ceasing and a thorough investigation of the general meaning. Our school’s current position clarifies that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) is revealed solely through the *Lotus Sūtra*;
it maintains that one contemplates a single thought-moment as being empty, provisional, and the Middle, which is the principle of signless concentration and wisdom.

Therefore, how could this [previous] judgment be erroneous? For within the treatise, the twenty-five expedient means (*upāya*) are extensively explained, and they are fully enumerated within the section on formal cultivation.
Regarding the ten objects that mutually arise within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the listing of the four *dhyānas* and eight *samādhis* each has its own specific purpose.

As in the section on skillful means (*upāya*), all are treated according to the principle of revelation, so that every instance of stillness (*śamatha*) and every instance of activity (*vipaśyanā*) is none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*).

Every skillful means is the true *dharmadhātu*, the wondrous practice of the mind-only. Having set forth these various objects, I fear that practitioners, in the course of their cultivation, might [become attached to them] due to the mind-only...

When the mind is engaged in sublime contemplation, latent habitual tendencies may be activated; if one fails to recognize their manifestations, one mistakes them for the teachings of the sages (as when a bhikṣu who has attained the four dhyānas claims to have attained the four fruits of the path).

The Great Master Zhizhe, therefore, sequentially demonstrated each of these states—including afflictions, karma, demons, and visions in meditation—so that practitioners might recognize the signs of what is being aroused within them.
By following this guidance, they realize that whatever arises is none other than the Truth itself.
The Dharma-gate of the Buddha’s Dharma-realm as Mind-Only is thus explained in exhaustive detail (the treatise exists and may be consulted for verification).

If one follows the judgment of Guifeng [Zongmi], it would be as if he were entirely refusing to allow the master Shuang to speak of the music of Zheng and Wei, or for Bole to describe the appearance of a common, slow horse.

If that were the case, then Guifeng’s own *Chanquan* (Explanations of Chan) would likewise be unfit to discuss the various characteristics of Chan practice; he could only have attained [a partial understanding].

This treatise concerns the school of non-conceptualization; since it explains the characteristics of various dhyāna practices, does it not cause the exegesis of Complete and Sudden Chan to become a gateway for gradual practice?
Moreover, as this exegesis of Chan lacks any intention to reveal and manifest [the ultimate truth], how far removed is it from the present *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation)?
Question: Is this the same as the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) and the *Zhi guan da yi* (General Meaning of Stopping and Contemplation)? Answer:

The *Jinbi* takes the eternal permanence of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as its central tenet. Jingxi [Zhanran] composed it to refute the worldly attachment to the view that external forms are not the Buddha-nature;

he extensively cited the original sūtras to interrogate and penetrate this point, subsequently establishing thirty-six topical gates before finally presenting a comprehensive response to reveal the Vairocana [Buddha-nature].
The nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction; this is no different from what is stated here.
The general meaning is specifically to extract the essential points of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* for Li Hua, directly revealing the inconceivable, which is precisely this "mind-only."
Question: Regarding the stages of the "six identities" elucidated in the preceding chapter, although the scriptural text is complete, their names and meanings remain obscure.

Since it is said that the dharma-realm is solely mind, can sentient beings know for themselves that they are already identical [to Buddhahood]? Answer: Within the inherent virtue of the dharma-realm, there is not even the name of "sentient being" or "Buddha";
who then could discuss identity or non-identity? One should know that "identity" refers to the Buddhas' knowledge of sentient beings.
The mind is originally Buddha, yet because it is not recognized in daily life, it is expediently pointed out by saying "it is right here.

Furthermore, the names of the "six identities" (*liu ji*) were established solely by the Tiantai school based on the *Lotus Sūtra* and other Mahāyāna scriptures, in order to manifest the stages of perfect enlightenment (*yuanwei*), wherein cultivation and nature, beginning and end, are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual, thus clarifying the relationship between cause and fruit. Therefore, Master Jingxi [Zhiyi] used the six...
Regarding the first of the three meanings established by these paired phrases, "identity" (*ji*) refers to identity because their principle is the same.
The single character "identity" (*ji*) points directly to the essence itself; it is like pointing to waves and saying they are water.

Thus, the *Sixteen Contemplations* states, "This mind is Buddha," and the *Samādhi of Seeing the Buddha* says, "To contemplate sentient beings as they truly are is to see them as Buddha. This is the Buddha of inherent nature (*xingde*).

"Because the matters are distinct, there are six": the single character "six" reveals that the matters of cultivation and nature, cause and effect, are distinct, just as pointing to water is itself pointing to waves.
Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says: "The Tathāgata dwells in immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, surpassing the pure conduct of all bodhisattvas.
Second, because the beginning and the end are both identical: "identical" means that all six stages are identical to Buddhahood.
It is also as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "The initial resolve and the ultimate goal are not two, for the beginning and the end do not overlap.

Sixth, the power and function of the noble ones and ordinary beings are as vastly separated as heaven and earth; as the *Sixteen Contemplations* states: "The mental conceptions of ordinary beings are weak and inferior;

If this were so, with what intent did the ancients interpret the "Expedient Means" chapter, judging its title and hanging it as a banner from of old, thereby misleading practitioners? This is all the more so when considering each and every dharma-characteristic of the Fundamental Gate.

Although the names and meanings differ slightly, how can one take the ten aspects of the non-duality of the traces (*ji*) and simply treat them as the fundamental reality (*ben-shi*) to explain it as non-duality?
The current names for the "ten non-dualities" are established merely by relying on the ten wonders (*shimiao*);
their titles may be combined or expanded, but this does not mean that one gate corresponds to one wonder. One should know that the ten gates encompass all ten wonders.
Thus, the causes and effects of both self and others are exhausted without exception. For this reason, Master Jingxi established the title for the text himself, stating:
"Since the Dharma and its doctrinal divisions have all been opened up to form the Sublime, these ten gates are titled 'Non-duality' (furni).
Here, "Dharma and its doctrinal divisions" refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*; the "ten gates" refers to the gates established based on the Ten Sublimities; and "non-duality" refers to—

Since the essential nature of the Dharma as described therein is warm and clear in its meaning, how could one suddenly contravene the texts established by the founding masters and arbitrarily apply the title "Non-duality of the Original and the Traces"?
Furthermore, the "Original and the Traces" are merely topical headings for the divisions of the scripture throughout antiquity and the present;
they are not the names of essential doctrinal characteristics (dharmalakṣaṇa) revealed in the sūtras and śāstras. How, then, could they be established as the tenth [category]?
This is the title for the "Sublime Non-duality. Furthermore, the concepts of "Original" (hon) and "Trace" (jaku) are precisely the master key for our school’s method of classifying the scriptures.
As the Preface to the *Xuan-yi* states: "The profound meaning is expressed through the 'mind of the text,' and there is nothing that surpasses the Original and the Trace;
because the Original and the Trace constitute the essential core, they are established as the title 'Non-duality. Regarding this, one might ask: did the Great Master Zhiyi not know [this]?

This expression regarding the "heart of the text" originates from Master Zhizhe (Zhang’an Chanshi), who used the metaphor of the lotus flower to illustrate the relationship between the Original and the Traces.
By applying the sixfold analogy of "opening what was closed" and "abolishing what was established," he attained the true purport of the sutra.
This is merely because the intention [of the text] lies precisely in the division of the sūtra’s sections; thus, the sūtra says, "Looking up at this principle, all meanings become clear.
How does this relate to the present *Ten Non-dual Gates*? Furthermore, although it introduces the topic, these are words concerning the "trace gate" (*jimon*);

therefore, establishing them as the non-duality of the fundamental and the trace (*honji*) makes it even clearer that one does not understand the meaning. It is simply for the sake of introducing the subject that it is stated in such a way.

This Trace Gate (Jikimon) cannot be titled "Fundamental and Trace" (Honjaku). Furthermore, if one were to say that non-duality (funi) is precisely the contemplation of mind, what harm would there be in using "Contemplating the Mind:
Fundamental and Trace" as the title? This is also not the case; moreover, a contemplation based on the text and attached to phenomena is not this principle of non-dual opposition.

Can one not hear that if one understands, then every character is liberation, but if one clings, then every word is a festering sore?

If one knows that the provisional and the real are non-dual, and simply realizes their meaning through the perfect spirit, why must one be shackled by their names and definitions? Now, regarding such people as these—

It is said that one should not grasp [at words]; yet if one speaks of the "extinction of marks," how can one discuss the fundamental and the manifest? If one proceeds to discuss the means of expression (*upāya*), how could names be established without their referents?

What I am discussing here concerns entirely what the Master of the True Doctrine has established; how could I be fabricating arguments of right and wrong?
