Question: Why did Master Jingxi establish these Ten Gates of Non-duality as verses, rather than composing them as a separate treatise?

Answer: In the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), he extensively elucidates the ten profundities (*shimiao*) of the Trace Gate through sixty rounds of the "provisional and ultimate" (*quan-shi*) and "relative and absolute" (*dai-jue*) distinctions.

Once the Profundity of the Fruit (*guomiao*) is completed, he again uses these sixty rounds of provisional and ultimate to resolve the various preceding profundities. He then states: "If one awakens to the Principle (*li*), then the Principle... [and so forth].

It is neither provisional nor real; not even a single dharma is perceived. It is like an empty fist deceiving a small child. To speak of the provisional and the real is to provide a dualistic explanation;

therefore, that which is neither provisional nor real is the "wondrous. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), in explaining the sixtyfold wondrousness mentioned above along with the discourse on the provisional and the real, concludes its explanation by stating: "Because all dharmas are extinguished and non-dual, it is further distinguished according to awakening."
The preceding ten chapters consist of the wondrous provisional and the real, the perfect and the one principle, and the nature of the mind; they are the consciousness that precedes [the realization].

Whether wondrous or coarse, whether opening or bestowing, the empty fist becomes the actual fruit. From this, the "Great Sound" (Laozi says: "The Great Sound is rarely heard") is established to manifest awakening.

Who would say it is for few? All are capable of being covered by the Perfect [Teaching]. From here, one enters the Gate of Non-duality (*advaya-mukha*); this is the profound trace-gate (*śeṣa-mukha*).
Is it not the case that the concluding text of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) indicates that awakening to the principle alone constitutes the "wondrous"?
Thus, by summarizing the general purport of the Ten Wondrousnesses (*shimiao*), it reveals their non-duality as the gateway for realization and entry. The text states:

"Therefore, I have extracted the Ten Wondrousnesses as the fundamental substance of the method of contemplation. This precisely articulates the intention of the author. The section on Question and Answer Resolving Doubts has already begun.
The title has been explained.

Second, regarding the interpretation of the text, first is the transcription of the original manuscript (this text was collated against many ancient versions by the *Shiqian* [Commentary on the Profound Meaning]; it was further verified and finalized through discussion with various eminent masters of the Teaching.

Nowadays, there exists a separately circulated version in which more than twenty characters differ; these likely resulted from three successive errors in transcription. Readers who have not yet examined this should consult the ancient version of the *Shiqian* for comparison, so as not to be led into much confusion). Here follows the latter section.
The detailed explanations are fully contained in the lower fascicle.

However, because this Trace Gate (*jìmén*) discusses cause and effect as well as self and other, so that the teachings of the entire lifetime of the Buddha may be harmonized and enter the Subtle, all the interpretations of its meanings are based upon the Four Teachings and the Five Flavors; the intent is that the teachings be opened up so that all may enter [the ultimate truth].

The Contemplation of the Mind as the Supreme Essence (Amṛta) is the pivotal mechanism of both teaching and practice; however, for now, it shall be briefly illuminated through reliance on various expositions.

Whether preserved or lost, these are not the primary intent of this specific section; thus, even where there are provisional arrangements—whether based on phenomena (*vastu*) or dharmas—they merely enumerate the ten contemplations by name.

The principles, objects, wisdom, practices, stages, and dharmas explained therein, as well as the means of transformation and those to be transformed, all reside within the expressive capacity of the teachings (*vyañjana*).
The "Middle" and "Pervasive" [sections] are wondrously intended to clarify the internal beginning and end, as well as the self and others;

thus, they fully expound the ten wonders, encompassing the general intent of the world-transcending teaching without exception. Therefore, one must understand the great outline of the ten wonders. Consequently, the ten wonders are summarized as the fundamental framework of the contemplative method.
If one understands the wonder of the traces and the wonder of the source, one should know that these are not remote from one another, but are merely matters of separation and combination.

The meaning of cause and effect is one; how can there be any difference between self and other? Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Though the original and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one.

Furthermore, since essence, doctrine, and function are merely the self, the other, cause, and effect, how much more so is the subsequent phase of the teaching merely a differentiation of the preceding four chapters?

If one understands this principle, then the teaching [will not be seen as] eternally distinct from the various texts of the preceding four chapters. If one is enlightened to this intent, then the teaching...

There is a single period of existence within which all horizontal and vertical phenomena do not transcend a single thought-moment; the three thousand worlds are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—the principle and the realm—and even the benefits [of practice] are entirely thus.

When this is so, the ten stages of the vehicle of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* constitute the cause and fruit of one's own cultivation (*sva-caryā*), while the chapter on "arousing the teaching" constitutes the agent and object of transforming others (*para-caryā*). Thus, self and other illuminate one another, the practice of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is perfected, and one's efforts shall not be in vain.

Since that which is expressed [by the teachings] can be known, these ten gates are further employed to subsume the Ten Profundities (*daśa-miāo*). What are they? Granting the provisional based upon the real means "duality within non-duality"; opening the provisional to reveal the real means "non-duality within duality. Since both the Dharma and the teaching sections are thus opened to become profound, these ten gates are titled "Non-duality," and beneath each gate, one should examine them through the six stages of realization (*liù jí*). **The Ten Gates of Non-duality:** 1. **The Gate of the Non-duality of Principle and Phenomena** (*lǐ shì bù èr mén*): Principle is the essence; phenomena are its function. Essence and function are neither identical nor different. 2. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Real and the Provisional** (*shí quán bù èr mén*): The real is the ultimate truth; the provisional is the conventional truth. Ultimate and conventional are neither the same nor distinct. 3. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Revealed and the Unrevealed** (*xiàn fēn bù èr mén*): The revealed is the explicit teaching; the unrevealed is the implicit meaning. Explicit and implicit are not two. 4. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Manifested and the Unmanifested** (*xiàn fēn bù èr mén*): The manifested is the visible form; the unmanifested is the invisible essence. Visible and invisible are non-dual. 5. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Expressed and the Unexpressed** (*shuō wèi bù èr mén*): The expressed is the verbal teaching; the unexpressed is the ineffable reality. Verbal and ineffable are one. 6. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Known and the Unknown** (*zhī wèi bù èr mén*): The known is the object of cognition; the unknown is the primordial nature. Object and nature are indivisible. 7.

**The Gate of the Non-duality of the Attained and the Unattained** (*dé wèi bù èr mén*): The attained is the fruit of practice; the unattained is the original state. Fruit and state are non-dual. 8. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Practiced and the Unpracticed** (*xíng wèi bù èr mén*): The practiced is the path of cultivation; the unpracticed is the inherent nature. Cultivation and nature are one. 9. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Teacher and the Taught** (*shī shòu bù èr mén*): The teacher is the guide; the taught is the recipient. Guide and recipient are not two. 10. **The Gate of the Non-duality of the Preacher and the Listener** (*shuō tīng bù èr mén*): The preacher is the expounder; the listener is the audience. Expounder and audience are non-dual. In each of these gates, one must verify the meaning by applying the principle of the six stages of realization (*liù jí*) to ensure that the distinction between the ordinary and the sage is clearly understood.

The preceding text has extensively cited authentic evidence; from here on, I shall simply set forth a single principle so that the essential purport of this entire scripture may be clearly manifest before one’s eyes:
first, the gate of the non-duality of form and mind; second, the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external; third, the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature;
fourth, the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect; fifth, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity; sixth, the gate of the basis...
The Seventh is the Gate of the Non-duality of Self and Other; the Eighth is the Gate of the Non-duality of the Three Karmas;

the Ninth is the Gate of the Non-duality of Expedient Means and Reality; and the Tenth is the Gate of the Non-duality of Receiving and Moistening. Among these, the first establishes its name based on the excellence of the object;
the second and third establish their names based on wisdom and practice; the fourth establishes its name based on the dharma of the stage; and the fifth... [and so forth].

The sixth and seventh [sections] are named after the supernatural powers of response and resonance; the eighth and ninth are named after the preaching of the Dharma; and the tenth is named after the benefits conferred upon the retinue.

Regarding the first, the "Gate of the Non-duality of Matter and Mind": among the ten suchnesses, from the realm of objects up to the ultimate truth (*anuttara-satya*), each possesses both a general and a specific meaning.
The general meaning resides in a single thought-moment, while the specific meaning distinguishes between matter and mind. Why is this so?

Regarding these, within the first ten [categories], characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain only to form (*rūpa*), while nature (*svabhāva*) pertains only to the substance of mind (*citta*). The function of acting as a condition (*pratyaya*) encompasses both mind and form;

cause and effect pertain only to mind, while retribution (*vipāka*) pertains only to form. Within the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), suffering (*duḥkha*) and karma (*karman*) encompass both, or they may pertain only to mind.

Regarding the four noble truths (*catvāri āryasatyāni*), three encompass both form and mind, while cessation (*nirodha*) pertains only to mind. Within the two truths (*dvayasatya*) and the three truths (*trisatya*), all are conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and fully possess form.

Within the true center of the mind, there is only the single reality of Mind-only, which is without reference point; this can be seen. Once one knows these distinctions, one integrates the particulars into the whole:
all dharmas are none other than the nature of mind. This single nature is a nature-less nature; the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest therein.

One should know that the form of the mind is the mind itself; "mind" is the name for transformation. Transformation is called "creation. "Creation" means identity of essence. Thus, it is neither form nor non-form.
Mind and form are mind; form is but mind. It is precisely because of this that we know there is only consciousness. When a single thought-moment arises, one perceives self and other as distinct.
Yet, since the Buddhas born of others are identical to one's own mind, how could the Buddhas born of oneself possibly deviate from that single thought-moment?
Thus, various objective phenomena are grasped without differentiation. Second, regarding the gate of the non-duality of internal and external: whatever object is contemplated...

It does not emerge from within or without; "without" refers to the marvelousness of that which relies upon and is manifested through form and mind—emptiness, the Middle Way, and the wondrous nature of emptiness.

Because the substance of mind and form is severed, there is only the single true nature. Within this, where emptiness, the provisional, and the Middle are non-existent, yet form and mind are vividly present, all is suddenly identical to true purity.

There are no longer sentient beings or the conceptualities of the seven stages of expedient means; one sees no distinctions between pure and defiled lands, for the sovereign [Buddha-nature] encompasses all that is relied upon.
Throughout the entire day it is brilliantly manifest. That which is called "internal" means first understanding external forms;

when the mind is in a single thought-moment of non-thought, one realizes that the internal essence itself is the three thousand realms as emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. Thus, external phenomena are entirely the nature of the mind. Since the nature of the mind has no exterior, its encompassing is all-pervasive.
The Dharma-realm of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the essential nature of sentient beings are no different; all are universally present—by whom could they not be?
Regarding the statement that "internal and external form and mind, as well as self and other, are used," this is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of form and mind.

Third, regarding the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature (*xiùxìng bùèrmén*): The nature-virtue (*xìngdé*) is precisely the *dharmadhātu* (the suchness of the realm) within a single thought-moment. Within this internal *dharmadhātu*, the three factors are fully present.

Although the nature is thus from the beginning, it is called "cultivation" by virtue of awareness. Cultivation illuminates the nature, and the nature gives rise to cultivation. When cultivation resides within the nature, it is entirely so.
In the cultivation of the arising of nature through practice, practice is entirely perfected by nature; nature does not shift, yet practice remains vividly present.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice: conforming practice and inverse practice. "Conforming" refers to realizing nature as one's conduct; "inverse" refers to turning one's back on nature to produce delusion.

Although the two minds of delusion and realization are non-dual, the natures of the inverse and conforming modes and their respective phenomena are eternally distinct. This is because while the phenomena do not shift the mind, the mind does not fail to manifest through the phenomena.

Thus, because delusion must be transformed into cultivation, perfected realization, and completion, one must undergo a single period of time to transform delusion into awakening and illumination into nature, thereby perfecting cultivation.

When both the cultivation of seeing nature and the cultivation of the mind are extinguished, one further understands that cultivation accords with nature through separation and union. "Separation" means that cultivation and nature each have three aspects;
"union" means that the two cultivations are one with nature, which is also threefold. Thus, although cultivation possesses nine aspects, [they are ultimately unified].
The nine *kṣetras* (stages) are threefold, which, for the sake of clarifying cultivation in relation to their nature, are combined into two types of cultivation;
these two and the one nature are like water and its waves. One should know that the nature refers to the three obstructions;

therefore, by means of the three cultivations, the nature is perfected, and the three dharmas are spontaneously realized. Upon reaching the state where there is no cultivation, the nature is the single, wondrous vehicle, free from all discrimination.

The Dharma-realm is profoundly luminous; this proclaims the gate of the non-duality of the internal and external, thus completing [the discussion]. Fourth, regarding the gate of the non-duality of cause and effect:
since the mind of sentient beings as the cause already possesses the three tracks (*trivartman*), when this cause achieves fruition, it is called the three nirvāṇas.

There is no distinction between cause and effect, for the principle is one from beginning to end. If this is so, why does the cause not abide in its own virtue? It is solely because of delusion regarding the cause that each [sentient being] remains [in saṃsāra].

This means that if one truly realizes that the nature of delusion is fundamentally nothing more than the abiding cause, then by long investigating this cause, the cause itself becomes manifest and is termed the "fruit.
Because the principle of cause and fruit is one, when this single principle is taken as the cause and its principle is fully revealed, there is no longer any name for "fruit.

How could the designation of "cause" still persist? Since both cause and fruit have vanished, the rational nature itself is extinguished; it is solely due to the extinction of wisdom—whether proximate or remote—that delusion is produced.

Because they form [the delusions of] thickness and thinness, and because they are confused by thickness and thinness, the meaning of the three afflictions is forcibly divided into six; this is because the levels of wisdom are opened up as shallow or deep.
It is like a dream where one exerts diligent effort: when the empty name of "affliction" is severed and the illusory cause is fulfilled, the mirror-image fruit becomes perfect.

Although the empty image and the real image are identical in principle, the empty is void while the image is substantial; because the substance of the image is real, it is called the fundamental reality, whereas the emptiness is void, and thus confusion revolves.
Nature is thus established as non-dual, yet dual as cause and effect; though dual, they are non-dual, for their essence is one from beginning to end.
If one claims the cause differs from the fruit, then the cause is not truly a cause. One must understand that the fruit proceeds from the cause, and only through the cause can the fruit be realized.

Thus, the three thousand realms existing within the principle are all termed "ignorance" (avidyā); when these three thousand realms are perfected as the fruit, they are all called "eternal bliss. These three thousand realms undergo no change.

"Clarification" refers to clarifying that the three bodies (*trikāya*) are both eternally identical in essence and identical in function; this is established through the gate of the non-duality of cultivation and nature.

Fifth, the gate of the non-duality of defilement and purity: If one recognizes that from the beginningless past the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) has been [mistakenly] taken as ignorance (*avidyā*), then one can now realize that ignorance itself is *dharmatā*. This *dharmatā*-ignorance universally creates all phenomena; this is termed "defilement."
The dharma-nature of ignorance universally accords with various conditions; it is designated as "turbid water" or "clear water.

Although there is no difference between the waves floating on them, and although turbidity arises from conditions, turbidity is fundamentally inherent; and although turbidity is fundamentally inherent, its entire substance is clarity.

Because the principle of these two waves applies to the whole substance being the function, the three thousandfold world of cause and effect is collectively termed "dependent origination" (paratantra-svabhāva) in the state of delusion.

Awakening to dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as inseparable from moment-to-moment [existence], one realizes that within each and every principle of this constant dependent origination, there is a distinction between the pure and the defiled:
six are defiled and four are pure. Yet, when considered universally, all ten are common to both the pure and the defiled.

Thus, one knows that although the defiled substance of each moment is entirely pure, because the three thousand realms have not yet been manifested and verified, the essence remains obscured; therefore, at the stage of semblance (sādṛśya-bhūmi), the six sense faculties radiate light universally.
The ten realms each possess [the three thousand] with utter clarity; how could it be that those who have purified the six sense organs claim that the ten [realms] are fixed as ten parts of reality?

Even when manifesting traces within the ten realms, it is likewise so because they are established through fruition as equal to those hundred realms. Therefore, from the very first moment of the mind, one must both negate and illumine:
because of illumination, the three thousand are eternally present; because of negation, they are by nature empty. Throughout the day, they are simultaneously absent and simultaneously manifest.
When this thought is stirred, it responds universally and without direction; according to what is felt, it bestows [its response], so that purity and defilement both vanish.

Because purity and defilement have vanished, one relies on emptiness and the Middle Way; yet, through emptiness and the Middle Way, one transforms defilement into purity. Because one realizes that within the emptiness of defilement and purity, they naturally vanish of themselves, the Gate of the Non-duality of Cause and Effect is thereby established.
Sixth, the Gate of the Non-duality of the Environment and the Sentient Beings: having already realized the *śūnyatā* (one-ness) of the obstructing and the penetrating...
The non-duality of essence arises precisely because from time immemorial, the three thousand realms are contained within a single thought-moment.

Within these three thousand, the two dharmas of the "middle" (the five aggregates) constitute the sentient beings, while the one thousand realms of the "outer" (the environment) belong to the land. Since both the sentient beings and the land abide within a single mind, how could this single mind be divided into subject and object?

Although there is no subject or object, the distinction between the sentient beings and the land remains perfectly distinct. Thus, through the two practices of the rational nature and the literal names, there exists a non-dual basis.

Because their characteristics are correctly established, the causes and effects of self and others mutually encompass one another. Although sentient beings have not yet manifested the fruit within the principle, everything is nonetheless the wondrous realm of Samantabhadra.
Nevertheless, one must further understand that the essence of the Buddhas' dharmas is neither partial nor biased, while the rational nature of sentient beings is neither restricted nor limited;
it remains unchanged from beginning to end, and there is no obstruction between the Great and Small Vehicles, as the principle of cause and effect is identical.
What distinguishes the "dependent" from the "correct"? Why would pure and defiled lands, superior and inferior bodies, the physical body and the Dharma-body be identical in measure?

Why would the dusty realm and the Land of Tranquil Light be no different? If this were so—that each single atom-land is all lands, and each single atom-body is all bodies—then their vastness, skillfulness, superiority, and inferiority would be inconceivable, and the locations of purity and defilement would be inexhaustible. This could not be otherwise than through the Three [Bodies].

How could the thousandfold emptiness, the provisional, and the middle establish such sovereign function? Only through this can one know that the sentient and the Buddha are equal, and that phenomena and principle mutually encompass one another.
This is established by way of the non-duality of defilement and purity. Seventh, regarding the gate of the non-duality of self and other:

the act of benefiting others according to their capacities relies upon the "fundamental foundation," which refers to the single nature being fully endowed with both self and other; only thus does one reach the fruition.

One’s own station is inherently beneficial to others, according to the principle of the three virtues and three truths within the three thousand realms. In one's own practice, these three thousand realms exist solely within the void; in benefiting others, the three thousand realms respond to sentient beings.
Although the capacities of sentient beings are immeasurable, the response does not exceed the three thousand realms. Although the modes of response are manifold, they do not exceed the ten realms.

Although the ten realms manifest through transformation, they do not exceed a single thought-moment. Although body and land arise in mutual interpenetration, they do not exceed the realm of serene light (sukhāvatī). Sentient beings [are likewise encompassed therein].
Because the principle (*li*) inherently possesses the three thousand [realms], it is able to evoke all Buddhas; because the principle of the three thousand is fulfilled, it is able to respond.
This response is directed toward specific capacities and accords with their particular inclinations, proceeding without error or deviation. How could this not be like a mirror manifesting images?

The mirror possesses the principle of manifesting images, while the form possesses the nature of producing an image. If a single form were unable to produce an image when facing the mirror, then the principle of the mirror would be exhausted, and the form would be deficient.
If a matter has not yet been realized, it may reasonably be so provided it is separated from a mirror; however, there is no physical form that does not reflect.
If a mirror fails to manifest an image, it is because it is obscured by dust; when the dust is removed by a person polishing it, the image appears. This is not due to the act of polishing itself.

By means of this analogy, the general principle of contemplating the Dharma can be understood: one must know that although the principle is inherently complete within both self and other, it necessarily relies upon conditions and causes.

The merit of benefiting others further arises from the union of the conditions (*pratyaya*), the causes (*hetu*), and the nature (*dharmatā*); only when these are integrated as one can the myriad phenomena be provisionally established in accordance with that nature.
Thus, the self-nature does not arise, and there is no fixed location; this is accomplished through the gate of the non-duality of the environment and its inhabitants.

If in this world there were only the Buddha-way, who would bestow the bodies of the three vehicles? Since even "body" is ultimately non-existent, speech must likewise not be speech.

When body and mouth are equal, they are identical to the mental wheel (*manas-cakra*). Mind and form are as one; transformation occurs without deliberation, eternally in profound accord with the ultimate.

Adapting actions to the capacities of beings—how could this not be the ten realms within a single thought-moment? Within each realm, there are no realms that are not the three karmas. Since even a single realm is the three karmas within a single thought-moment, how could it be otherwise?

The function of the sublime fruit is never deficient, for the cause must correspond to the fruit. Only through faith can one know that the three mysteries have their source in the fact that the three karmas of the ten realms are all empty, provisional, and middle; thus, they respond appropriately and exclusively to serve as the fruit.

Each manifested form and each spoken sound is not without the self-sufficient transformation of the three karmas of the ten realms, and these transformations further produce further transformations—is this not what is meant? Therefore, the One...

One should reflect that the ordinary mind already possesses the principle of the ocean of the three mysteries; that the retributive form within a single speck of dust is identical to the fundamental principle;

The ninth, the Gate of the Non-duality of Expedient Means and Reality: Equal Great Wisdom constantly mirrors the Dharma-realm; it arises from the nine expedients and one reality within the principle of nature (*dharmatā*).
Reality is further the nine realms, and expedient means is likewise so. Expedient means and reality are mutually merged; within a single thought-moment, the hundred realms cannot be distinguished.
This spontaneous, constant state reaches fruition through the realization of the fundamental single principle—a state that is neither expedient nor real.

The provisional and the real are precisely as described above: through the mastery of the mind-wheel, one causes body and speech to respond to the capacities of beings according to the provisional and the real.

Thus, the three karmas are in accord with the provisional and the real in a single thought-moment; they are applied without moving from the provisional or the real, so how could there be any separation or distinction between them?

It is precisely by means of the provisional and the real that names are established, and it is precisely in the person that the True and the Responsive are manifested. Since the principle of the three karmas is identical, the provisional and the real are in profound union.

The gate of the non-duality of the three karmas is established; as for the gate of the non-duality of the ten types of moisture-nourishment: the fundamental nature of dharmas inherently possesses both the provisional and the real.
Through beginningless habitual perfuming, these may manifest as either real or provisional. Provisional and real are equal in principle due to this perfuming;

when the appropriate conditions are met, they form habits, supported by practice and vows. If there were no original cause, even perfuming would be in vain. When meeting with perfuming, they appear distinct from one another, yet they are not [ultimately] so.

Although their natures are distinct, and though these natures themselves possess no differentiation, they must rely upon illusion to give rise to illusory capacity, illusory resonance, illusory response, and illusory arrival.

Both the one who responds and those who are transformed are neither provisional nor ultimate; yet, because sentient beings possess a capacity that is neither provisional nor ultimate, they become the vehicle for the provisional and the ultimate.

The Buddha likewise possesses a fruition that is neither provisional nor ultimate, thereby serving as the response that is both provisional and ultimate. When the capacity of beings and the response coincide, the manifested bodies and lands are impartial and identical.

Since the eternal, quiescent light is not anything other than the Dharma-realm, one knows that the three thousand worlds are co-present within the mind-ground; thus, the three thousand worlds in the Buddha’s mind-ground are no different from those in [one's own] mind-ground.

The four subtle elements are identical in essence, and their provisional and real aspects are equal in benefit. This is established by means of the gate of the non-duality of the provisional and the real.

Therefore, through these ten gates, one universally enters into both form and mind, and even unto the moisture of the *dharmadhātu*; because all are thus, the ten wondrous aspects (*daśa-prakāra*) are of a single principle from beginning to end.
The initial object is primordially complete; by relying on the three [truths], understanding arises from the principle, and is thus called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).

Wisdom and understanding guide practice, and the union of practice, understanding, and principle accords with the reality. Although these three factors correspond and are not different, provisional designations of shallow and deep are established to distinguish their respective positions and avoid confusion.
The Dharma is precisely the realization of that principle. [From] the fifth chapter of the third section downward, there are three chapters on the arising of the function of the three dharmas.

The sentient beings are immeasurable—each being a trichiliocosm—and even unto the Buddhas, they are immeasurable—each being a single trichiliocosm.

and the single thought-mind is called the non-dual middle. This is called the "three contemplations in a single mind. Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* says: "It is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle."
